title: Act I, Scene I
focus: the street brawl and lovesick Romeo

teacherSummary.text: Capulet servants Sampson and Gregory provoke Montague servants; Benvolio tries to part them, Tybalt attacks him, and a general brawl draws in citizens and the old heads of both houses. Prince Escalus stops it and decrees death for the next disturbance. Benvolio then finds Romeo moping: he loves Rosaline, who has sworn to stay chaste.

significance: The scene establishes the feud's absurd energy, the Prince's death sentence that will make Romeo's later fight fatal, and Romeo's habit of falling in love with language as much as with a person.
discussionQuestions: What makes small insults turn into big fights? Think of an example from school or the news.

How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with violence and the feud?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act I, Scene I,” how does Shakespeare show the street brawl and lovesick Romeo? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act I, Scene I, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the street brawl and lovesick Romeo? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the conflict in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act I, Scene I develops the idea of the street brawl and lovesick Romeo. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act I, Scene I (where it begins, turns and ends) and its conflict shape the reader's understanding of the street brawl and lovesick Romeo. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act I, Scene I suggests about the street brawl and lovesick Romeo. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's conflict and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses conflict in Act I, Scene I to complicate the reader's understanding of the street brawl and lovesick Romeo. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act I, Scene I within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the street brawl and lovesick Romeo responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act I, Scene I alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the street brawl and lovesick Romeo follows or bends those conventions, using the conflict as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene I and its treatment of the street brawl and lovesick Romeo. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's conflict and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene I as evidence for a larger claim about the street brawl and lovesick Romeo in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene I as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the street brawl and lovesick Romeo. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

Why, such is love’s transgression.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “Madam, an hour before the worshipp’d sun / Peer’d forth the golden window of the east, / A troubled mind” (Act I, Scene I, Benvolio (speech 55)).

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
